strengths: Strong predictive performance on held-out interventions (Pearson r=0.67±0.14 vs. 0.03 for baselines), demonstrating genuine ability to predict effects of unseen perturbations
Impressive scalability to 817 genes compared to competitors limited to ~100 genes; practical advantage for high-dimensional genomics
Biologically grounded neural ODE formulation with thoughtful design choices (Hill function equivalence, RNA decay, gene modules) that connect to established biology
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across simulated (400-gene yeast, 100-gene random) and real (TF Atlas) datasets with multiple metrics and detailed ablations
Interpretable two-layer factorization (G=A·diag(α)·B) providing gene-module-gene decomposition useful for biological understanding
Clear presentation with good intuition for methods and informative visualizations
weaknesses: Critical theoretical gap: Identifiability not rigorously proven for the deterministic ODE case; defers to future work ('Authors 2025') despite being fundamental to causal interpretation of learned parameters

Severe over-prediction with fragile thresholding: Predicts ~43,000 edges vs. 623 ground truth (6,900% over-prediction); requires dataset-specific threshold tuning (c=0.1 vs. c=0.01), suggesting learned GRN is implicitly dense
Modest inference performance on real data: Recall ~50% on TF Atlas with only 50-70% edge recovery across bootstrap replicates; validation uses only 3 tiny networks (3-4 TF networks) from literature
Simulated data does not establish superiority: DCDI matches or outperforms PerturbODE on 400-gene yeast (AUPRC ~3×10⁻³ vs 2.5×10⁻³); advantage only when DCDI fails to scale, not on accuracy
Limited biological validation: Only 7 of 200 modules analyzed; unclear if other 193 modules are biologically meaningful; gene enrichment validation is suggestive but not definitive
Incomplete baselines: No comparison to regression-based methods (GENIE3, GRNBoost2) mentioned in introduction; missing comparison to recent causal representation learning approaches
Over-claimed results: Titles and framing emphasize 'GRN discovery' with 50% recall as success; predictive strength on held-out interventions is the genuine contribution but is somewhat downplayed
Reproducibility concerns: No mention of code availability; identifiability analysis should be in main text; arbitrary hyperparameter choices (module number 200, λ=0.001) lack sensitivity analysis

strengths: Demonstrates practical scalability to ~800 genes on TF Atlas, outperforming DCDI and Bicycle on real data
Successfully predicts effects of held-out transcription factor perturbations with Pearson r=0.67 vs -0.03 for linear baseline methods

Gene modules show coherent biological interpretation, with enrichment for known developmental pathways (anterior-posterior axis, vascular endothelial differentiation) and p-values <0.001 against random graphs
Comprehensive evaluation including multiple simulated datasets, real data, extensive ablations, stability and generalizability analyses
Technically sound implementation of neural ODEs with appropriate loss functions (Wasserstein-2 distance) and clear mathematical formulation
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: combines well-established neural ODE technique (Chen et al., 2018) with classical gene module networks (Segal et al., 2005); core contribution of factorizing G=A·diag(α)·B is incremental

Weak justification for causal claims: identifiability section defers to unpublished paper with no rigorous proof in submission; allows cycles (contradicting causal DAG assumptions) while claiming causal discovery; no discussion of confounding

Poor empirical performance on SERGIO benchmarks: DCDI outperforms on 400-gene yeast data (AUPRC 0.004 vs 0.003); marginal improvement on 100-gene random DAGs; paper dismisses underperformance due to DCDI scaling issues rather than addressing it directly

Severe over-prediction problem: predicts 43,655 edges vs 623 ground truth (yeast, 400 genes), implying >99% false discovery rate; L1 penalty on B alone insufficient since G=A·diag(α)·B is not necessarily sparse when multiplying sparse matrices

Limited validation on real data: only 3 curated GRNs evaluated from TF Atlas; modest recall 35-50%; unrealistic assumption of positive-only edges (actual GRNs contain both activating and repressing); no explanation for low recall or practical utility

Low consistency in edge recovery: bootstrap/split analysis shows only 50-70% stability (Figure 22), undermining reliability for discovering causal relationships; paper acknowledges this is 'less than ideal' without adequately addressing implications

Misuse of ODE formulation: TF Atlas provides single timepoint per perturbation (day 0 and day 7), not trajectories; paper never justifies why ODE modeling is necessary versus simpler static models that don't require time-integration assumptions

Inconsistent thresholding across baselines (PerturbODE c=0.1 for 400 genes vs c=0.01 for 100 genes; DCDI=0.5, NO-TEARS=0.3, Bicycle=0.005) making fair comparison difficult; different hyperparameters (modules: 100 vs 200) for different methods
Missing recent baselines: no comparison to Scribe, CellOracle, or 2023-2024 methods; limited engagement with Hossain et al. (2024) neural ODE work mentioned in related work

No code availability mentioned; key practical contribution (log1p transformation achieving 'substantial improvement') relegated to appendix; limited ablation on hyperparameter sensitivity despite many dataset-specific choices

strengths: Well-motivated framework grounding in biology: gene modules reduce dimensionality while reflecting established biological principles; Hill function approximation and decay terms show domain expertise
Strong scalability: handles 817 genes on TF Atlas while DCDI and Bicycle fail, demonstrating practical value
Impressive held-out prediction results: Pearson r = 0.67±0.14 vs 0.03±0.01 for competitors; compelling W₂ distance improvements with supporting visualizations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple datasets (simulated and real), held-out interventions, extensive ablations, stability/generalizability analysis with 10⁵ bootstraps

Interpretable gene modules: seven discovered modules align with known biology (anterior-posterior axis, trophoblast/endothelial specification); gene enrichment analysis provides independent validation
Principled intervention modeling: well-designed masking formulation for knockouts and shift terms for overexpression
Extensive reproducibility details: comprehensive appendix with hyperparameters, extended results, and experimental specifications
weaknesses: Unresolved identifiability: lacks formal proof for deterministic ODE case; cites incomplete 'Authors (2025)' reference; identifiability claim (interventions > dimension) unjustified; fundamental theoretical gap
Severe edge over-prediction: predicts 43,655 edges vs 623 ground truth (70× overprediction) despite significant p-values; explanation (sparse matrix multiplication) acknowledged but unsolved
Modest edge selection stability: only 50-70% recovery of ground truth edges in bootstrap stability analysis, falling short of acknowledged 75% threshold for reliability
Threshold selection concerns: different c values (0.1 vs 0.01) across experiments; Bicycle threshold 'discovered empirically'; potential for inflation of comparative advantages
Mixed simulation results: DCDI outperforms on controlled experiments (400-gene: 0.0059 vs 0.0044 AUPRC; 100-gene: marginal); PerturbODE advantage mainly at dimensions where DCDI fails
Absent formal theoretical guarantees: no parameter identifiability proof, no GRN recovery conditions, claimed SCM equivalence via stable fixed points unproven
Limited neural ODE baseline comparison: Jackson et al. (2023) and Hossain et al. (2024) cited but not directly compared
Incomplete module interpretation: only 7 of 200 modules thoroughly analyzed; no systematic false positive assessment; generalizability unclear
Missing computational analysis: no runtime comparisons; scalability limits unexplored; can it handle 5000+ genes?
Incomplete time course analysis: TF Atlas fixed at 7 days; sensitivity to endpoint choice unexplored
Inadequate failure case analysis: some interventions have W₂>300 despite average ~84 (Table 2) without investigation of difficulty factors
Limited noise handling: deterministic ODE inappropriate for stochastic biology; diffusion regularization helps but lacks formal treatment; no uncertainty quantification

strengths: Addresses important scalability problem: Successfully handles 812 genes on real TF Atlas data where existing methods (DCDI, Bicycle) fail due to memory constraints

Elegant and biologically-grounded methodology: Factorized graph structure G = A·diag(α)·B reduces parameters while maintaining interpretability; appropriate use of Hill functions and decay terms for biological realism

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple simulated benchmarks, large-scale real data experiments, statistical testing against Erdős-Rényi random graphs, GSEA validation, ablation studies, and stability/generalizability analyses

Demonstrable interpretability: Successfully recovers known developmental GRNs (anterior-posterior axis, trophoblasts, vascular endothelium) through discovered modules with statistically significant alignment (p < 0.001)

Appropriate technical choices: Wasserstein-2 OT loss for distribution matching without cell correspondence, L1 sparsity justified by network motif prevalence, novel diffusion-based regularization for stability
weaknesses: Identifiability concerns undermine causal claims: Authors acknowledge identifiability is 'somewhat delicate' but defer proof to unpublished 2025 preprint; claim identifiability holds 'in principle' when #interventions > dimension lacks rigor; without identifiability guarantees, causal interpretation of parameters is fundamentally questionable

Mixed performance on core GRN inference task: Underperforms NO-TEARS and GENIE3 on small problems (10-100 genes); comparable to DCDI at moderate scales; only shows clear advantage where other methods fail due to computational constraints—suggesting scalability rather than accuracy improvement

Inferior prediction accuracy on unseen interventions: W2 distance of 84±88 significantly worse than GEARS (65±7.3); much higher variance (88 vs 7.3) indicates instability; outperformed on core generalization task despite claims of predictive capability

High false discovery rates and threshold sensitivity: Table 1 shows FDR of 50-58% at medium-high sparsity; no principled threshold selection (different c values required for different datasets); number of predicted edges varies dramatically (50k-200k) with hyperparameter changes (Figure 14)

Poor stability and generalizability: Bootstrap analysis (Figure 28) recovers ground truth edges only 50-70% of the time; authors acknowledge ideally should exceed 75%; raises serious doubts about reliability of specific discovered edges

Limited module-level interpretability: Only 7 of 200 modules align with known GRNs (Figure 22); Figure 26 shows many modules redundantly enrich for identical pathways; unclear what other ~193 modules represent or whether they represent overfitting

Comparison and evaluation design issues: Different thresholds applied to different methods complicating fair comparison; treating incorrect sign predictions as false positives may underestimate PerturbODE; NO-TEARS/LR predict near-empty graphs (0.2-0.4 edges) making comparison uninformative

strengths: Addresses an important problem combining trajectory inference with causal discovery

Identifiability discussion relegated to single paragraph citing anonymous 2025 paper; no rigorous proof or validation that parameters are identifiable
Interpretability claims inadequately supported: only 7/200 modules show high enrichment; gene modules lack systematic validation as corresponding to biological structures
No direct comparison with relevant neural ODE baselines (Hossain et al. 2024, Jackson et al. 2023)
Stability analysis (Appendix A.15) shows ground-truth edges selected only 50-70% of the time—below acceptable reliability thresholds

strengths: Well-motivated biological approach combining neural ODEs with causal discovery, grounded in Hill functions and module-based GRN architecture
Exceptional scalability: handles 812 genes versus ~400 for DCDI and memory limits for Bicycle, with demonstrated convergence on large-scale TF Atlas dataset
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple simulated datasets (SERGIO, BoolODE), real data (TF Atlas with 1.1M cells), six baseline methods, extensive ablations and hyperparameter studies
Sound technical framework: clear ODE decomposition (Eq. 1-2), optimal transport loss for distribution matching, handling both perfect and imperfect interventions
Biologically interpretable results: inferred modules align with known developmental pathways (anterior-posterior axis, angiogenesis) validated through GSEA with p-values <0.001
Practical capability to predict effects of held-out interventions with Wasserstein distance competitive with or outperforming specialized methods
Excellent reproducibility: comprehensive appendix with hyperparameters, detailed experimental protocols, stable convergence plots, and code repository references
weaknesses: Identifiability not rigorously proven: relies on forthcoming work for theoretical guarantees; ODE case identifiability only claimed 'in principle' when interventions exceed gene dimension, lacking formal proof

GRN extraction mapping incompletely justified: claimed G = A diag(α)B captures network structure, but nonlinearities (sigmoid, bias term β) and transient dynamics aren't fully accounted for in this linear decomposition

Moderate absolute performance on real data: recall ~0.40-0.50 (missing ~50% of edges) and FDR ~50-55% on TF Atlas limits practical utility; unstable edge recovery (50-70% consistency in Appendix A.15, deserves prominence)
Limited dynamics information: only day 0 and day 7 measurements used; two time points insufficient to learn true temporal trajectories or reliably distinguish direct from indirect effects

Arbitrary modularity: number of modules (100-200) chosen empirically without principled justification; performance plateaus but unclear whether modules represent true biology or flexible parameter fitting

Narrow experimental scope: only TF overexpression perturbations tested; generalization to CRISPR knockdown and other perturbation types unknown; ground truth validation only on 223/812 genes (ChIP-Atlas)

Unfair baseline comparisons in some settings: comparing nonlinear method to linear methods (NO-TEARS, NO-TEARS-LR) gives inherent advantage; more relevant comparison is DCDI where PerturbODE doesn't uniformly dominate (DCDI wins on 400-gene yeast AUPRC)
Key ablations missing: contributions of log1p transformation, gene selection strategy, and diffusion-based regularization (Section 3.4) not isolated; unclear which components are essential
Stability and generalization concerns (Appendix A.15): ground truth edges recovered only 50-70% of time across bootstrap samples and train-test splits, suggesting variable network structure learning
